metrics.title: Q2 2026 Revenue
metrics.label: +49% YoY, beat ~$6.85B consensus — first public quarter. Starlink $3.94B (+51% YoY), Launch $1.76B (+46% YoY, 47 orbital flights), SpaceXAI $1.08B (+85% YoY). Group adj. EBITDA $2.08B (~29% margin); GAAP net loss $(1.38)B.

metrics.title: Starlink Engine
metrics.label: Q2 2026 — 12.1M subs (+17% QoQ from 10.3M Q1), ARPU $69/mo (up from $66 on May price hike), $1.44B operating income (+21% QoQ). The monetisation pivot is working: revenue grew faster than subs for the first time since the international mix shift.

metrics.title: AI Segment — Grok 4.5
metrics.label: Contracted run-rate after the July 8 Grok 4.5 launch — Q2 SpaceXAI revenue was $1.08B (+85% YoY) but the segment lost $(920)M adj. EBITDA on Colossus depreciation. Anchor deals: ~$1.25B/mo Anthropic, ~$920M/mo Google through 2029. Revenue ramps from Q3; margin stays negative near term.

moat.description: Reusable-rocket cost monopoly (82% of global launch) plus the Starlink spectrum-and-scale flywheel — unchanged by the Q2 print; the earnings confirmed the physical moat is compounding, not eroding.
moat.analysisSummary: SpaceX's durability is physical and regulatory, not software. Two reinforcing engines:

analysisPoints.title: Reusable-Launch Cost Monopoly
analysisPoints.text: 165 orbital launches in 2025 (82% global share) on a fleet of reusable Falcon boosters — one flew a 29th time. Q2 2026 added a record 47 orbital flights in a single quarter. No competitor (Blue Origin, Rocket Lab, ULA, China) has matched orbital-class reuse at cadence, giving SpaceX a structural cost-per-kg advantage measured in years, not quarters.

analysisPoints.title: Spectrum + Orbital Slots
analysisPoints.text: Starlink's FCC spectrum grants and ITU orbital-slot filings are scarce, first-mover, government-allocated assets. A rival cannot simply out-spend its way past the regulatory queue — this is the single hardest part of the moat to replicate.

analysisPoints.title: The Self-Funding Flywheel
analysisPoints.text: SpaceX launches its own constellation at internal cost, so every Falcon flight makes Starlink cheaper to deploy, and Starlink cash flow funds the next constellation tranche and Starship. Vertical integration competitors must buy launch on the open market to compete.

growth.description: Q2 2026 (reported August 4) was SpaceX's first public earnings and it delivered a clean beat on the core: revenue $7.18B (+49% YoY vs. ~$6.85B consensus), led by Starlink $3.94B (+51% YoY) on 12.1M subs and a stabilising $69/mo ARPU after the May price hike — the first quarter where revenue outpaced subscriber growth since the international mix shift. Launch hit a record 47 orbital flights ($1.76B, +46% YoY). SpaceXAI contributed $1.08B (+85% YoY) but lost $(920)M adj. EBITDA; Grok 4.5 launched July 8, after quarter-end, so the ~$27.8B/yr contracted compute book ramps from Q3, not Q2. Management raised FY2026 revenue guidance to $31–33B (from the IPO prospectus $28–32B band) but also lifted capex to $25–27B (from $24–26B), keeping FCF deeply negative — the stock rallied ~4% on the Starlink beat and retraced after-hours on the spend step-up, closing August 4 at ~$151. Starship flew 3 orbital test flights in H1 2026, on pace for the 8-flight full-year target (vs. 5 in all of 2025) — progress, not proof.

growthAnalysis.scoreDerivation: Base 91 (~35% blended CAGR, 30%+ band) + 5 recurring (Starlink subscription base, 12M+ and compounding) + 4 both (direct-to-cell + AI-compute TAM expansion on top of share gains) + ~3 trajectory (Starlink and launch accelerating on Q2 beat) − 10 high risk (Starship execution, FCF burn, AI segment losses) − 12 margin compressing (group adj. EBITDA margin fell to ~29% in Q2 from ~35% FY2025 on AI capex drag) = 81. Q2 beat confirms Starlink monetisation and launch cadence; Grok 4.5 contract book de-risks the AI leg from Q3 but does not earn margin credit yet; Starship H1 progress (3 flights) is noted but severity stays high until ≥15/yr cadence is demonstrated.

drivers.name: Starlink Broadband
drivers.metric: Q2 2026 $3.94B (+51% YoY, +21% QoQ); 12.1M subs; $1.44B op profit; ARPU $69/mo post-May hike

drivers.name: Launch Services
drivers.metric: Q2 2026 $1.76B (+46% YoY); record 47 orbital launches in quarter; ~$22B cumulative federal contracts

drivers.name: Direct-to-Cell + AI Compute
drivers.metric: D2C carrier deals reaching ~7–8M users; SpaceXAI Q2 $1.08B (+85% YoY); Grok 4.5 (Jul 8) anchors ~$27.8B/yr contracted compute ramping Q3+

growthAnalysis.keyRisk: Starship is the linchpin of the next constellation generation and the cost curve. H1 2026 delivered 3 orbital test flights — on pace for the 8-flight 2026 target and an improvement on 2025's 5-of-25 miss — but reliable orbital-class reuse at ≥15 launches/yr is still unproven. If Starship does not reach that cadence by end of 2027, V3 Starlink deployment and the launch-cost step-down slip, undercutting both the $60B run-rate bull case and the FCF turn the ~$2T valuation requires.

valuation.description: At ~$151 (August 4 close, +4% on the Q2 beat, retracing after-hours on the raised capex guide) SPCX has recovered from the July 10 all-time low of ~$145 but now sits essentially at the $155 base case — the post-earnings bounce closed the modest discount that existed at the July 19 review. The first public print confirmed Starlink monetisation and raised FY2026 revenue guidance to $31–33B, partially de-risking the forward run-rate, but the simultaneous capex lift to $25–27B reminded the market that GAAP losses and deeply negative FCF persist. At ~95× trailing sales / ~270× EV/EBITDA the stock remains among the richest large-caps; earnings multiples are still meaningless on a $(1.38)B quarterly GAAP loss. The margin of safety that existed at $145 is largely gone — the market now pays fair value for flawless Starlink execution and prices the AI-compute ramp as backlog, not yet as margin.

valuationNote.text: P/E is omitted — SpaceX is GAAP loss-making ($(1.38)B net loss in Q2 2026; $(4.94)B in FY2025) and FCF-negative ($2.1B OCF vs. $6.4B Q2 capex), so earnings multiples are meaningless. Valuation is anchored on price/sales (~95× trailing, ~60–65× 2026E on the raised $31–33B guide) and EV/EBITDA (~$2.0T vs. ~$8.3B annualised adj. EBITDA ≈ 240×). The premium is paid for monopoly cost position, spectrum, Grok/AI-compute optionality, and Mars/Starship — not current cash generation.
valuationNote.fairValue: $155 (base) — stock now trades at fair value after the Q2 beat closed the post-IPO discount

bear.description: Growth-stock derating meets lock-up supply and execution slips: the market stops paying ~110× sales for a GAAP-loss, dual-class-controlled company, and Starship disappointments compound into a permanent re-rate toward ~$1.3T.
points: Post-IPO lock-up expiries (2026–27) flood the thin ~3% float with insider supply as the Nasdaq-100 forced-buying bid fades
Starship keeps missing cadence targets through 2027 (as in 2025's 5-of-25), delaying V3 Starlink and the launch-cost step-down
Even after the May 2026 hike, Starlink ARPU re-rolls over and net adds slow as Amazon Kuiper reaches commercial scale, capping broadband growth below 30%

base.description: Starlink scales and monetises (post-hike ARPU stabilises), launch dominance holds, and the newly-contracted AI-compute book ramps but stays loss-making on Grok's sub-cost pricing — capex keeps FCF negative and the stock holds near its ~$1.9–2.0T level.
points: 2026 revenue lands in the raised $31–33B guide on Starlink ~$18–22B (12M+ subs compounding) plus record launch volume, with the ~$27.8B/yr AI-compute contracts (Anthropic, Google) ramping from Q3 and adjusted EBITDA margin holding ~28–32%
The May 2026 price increase sticks, stabilising ARPU in the high-$60s and lifting Starlink operating margin even as subscribers grow — as Q2 demonstrated

Grok 4.5 wins share on price but the AI segment stays GAAP-negative on Colossus depreciation, and Starship reaches orbital reuse below 15/yr — so the full cost-curve and FCF turn arrive later than bulls assume

bull.description: The flywheel inflects on all cylinders: Starship hits cadence, Starlink + D2C compound with firming ARPU, and AI-compute contracts materialise toward a ~$60B run-rate, re-rating the company toward ~$3.2T.
points: Starship reaches ≥15 launches/yr with reliable reuse, collapsing $/kg and enabling V3 Starlink mass deployment

Grok 4.5's Opus-class benchmarks and price advantage convert the ~$27.8B/yr contract book into a durable franchise, and AI-compute/connectivity (enterprise/defence, orbital data centres from 2028) drives the exit-2026 run-rate toward $60B
Starlink crosses ~20M subscribers with ARPU rising post-hike, and free cash flow turns positive, validating a premium growth multiple

learnedInterfaces.note: launch is a contracted service and the Starlink terminal is deliberately plug-and-play. There is no complex interface customers invest years mastering.

businessLogic.note: SpaceX does not embed configurable software into customers' proprietary workflows. Launch and broadband are procurement/utility relationships, not business-logic lock-in.

publicDataAccess.note: the company does not monetise gated access to a public dataset.

talentScarcity.note: Reusable-orbital propulsion, GNC, and large-scale satellite-manufacturing expertise is the scarcest engineering talent in aerospace, and SpaceX has assembled the only team operating it at cadence. AI augments but does not replace rocket and spacecraft engineers — this scarcity is AI-resilient.

bundling.note: Vertical integration is the bundle: in-house launch deploys Starlink at internal cost, ground network plus terminal plus connectivity is sold as one stack, and D2C bundles satellite into carrier plans. Competitors must assemble these pieces on the open market. AI-compute/connectivity is an emerging extension of the same bundle.

proprietaryData.note: 500+ Falcon flights and 29× booster reuse generate proprietary reliability, recovery, and reuse telemetry no rival possesses, plus a continuous stream of constellation operations data. The xAI merger adds the Colossus I/II gigawatt clusters and Grok 4.5's frontier weights, fed by captive Tesla-fleet and SpaceX-engineering data — but frontier-model weights commoditise and Grok competes on price, so this leg is AI-vulnerable and does not deepen durability. Kept intact: the data is real and compounding, but it improves operations rather than being a directly-monetised, defensible product.

regulatoryLockIn.note: FCC spectrum grants, ITU orbital-slot priority, FAA launch licences, and NASA/DoD national-security launch certification are scarce, slow, first-mover-advantaged assets. Switching launch providers requires re-certification, and spectrum/slots cannot be out-spent past the regulatory queue. This is the hardest moat to replicate and is AI-irrelevant.

networkEffects.note: Upgraded from weakened (Jul 19 2026 review). Added users on a Starlink cell still congest shared capacity rather than improve it — the classic per-user effect is absent — but two ecosystem-level effects are demonstrably present: the self-funding launch↔Starlink flywheel (every Falcon flight lowers constellation deployment cost, every Starlink dollar funds more launch, and third-party rideshare demand deepens the same cost curve), and the direct-to-cell two-sided network now signing carriers (~7–8M reachable users; more carriers → more coverage → more attractive to the next carrier). Q2's record 47 launches and Starlink profit expansion reinforce the flywheel without changing the rating — it was already intact. Not strong: D2C is early and the per-user effect never arrives.

transactionEmbedding.note: SpaceX does not sit in a payment or transaction layer.

systemOfRecord.note: it is not the authoritative record for any external business function.

tenMoats.verdict: SpaceX is a net AI beneficiary on the demand side — AI buildout drives launch demand, satellite connectivity, and, since the xAI merger, an in-house frontier-model and compute franchise (Grok 4.5, Colossus) with a ~$27.8B/yr contracted book — while its core moats (regulatory spectrum/slots, scarce aerospace talent, reusable-launch cost position) are essentially AI-irrelevant and therefore AI-resilient. The Grok/AI leg is the exception: it is a genuine growth and cash driver but the single AI-vulnerable part of the business — frontier weights commoditise, Grok competes on price, and the segment is deeply loss-making — so it lifts growth optionality without deepening the moat, which is why the moat score is unchanged after the Q2 print. It still carries almost none of the AI-vulnerable software moats (no learned interface, business-logic, public-data, transaction, or system-of-record exposure), so AI cannot erode the physical/regulatory durability it has. The honest limitation is that half the moat slate is N/A — the framework's heavyweight software categories structurally don't apply — and network effects, though upgraded to intact on the launch↔Starlink flywheel and the emerging direct-to-cell two-sided network, are ecosystem-deep rather than classic per-user effects. Durable physical/regulatory monopoly, but not a software-style compounder.
